title: Effectiveness of Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop Generate–Validate–Repair for Natural‑Language → Configuration Translation in Emulated Multi‑Device Networks
abstract: We investigate whether an iterative generate–validate–repair workflow that places a formal network verifier (Batfish) in the loop reduces semantic configuration errors when an LLM translates operator intents into multi‑device configuration changes. Following a preregistered paired design (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001), we sampled N=200 confirmatory multi‑device intents (stratified by topology size) and compared a single‑pass LLM generation (baseline) to a bounded verifier‑guided repair pipeline (guarded). Open‑source emulation (FRRouting/VyOS images in containerized Mininet‑style networks) and a deterministic validator produced paired binary semantic outcomes (pass/fail). All confirmatory pairs completed (200/200); baseline and guarded conditions both achieved 200/200 verifier‑pass outcomes (paired absolute difference = 0.00; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]). These confirmatory results are therefore null with respect to the preregistered hypotheses because the baseline already produced verifier‑passing artifacts in this execution. Exploratory analyses were limited by this ceiling effect. We report detailed execution artifacts, deterministic failure and contamination checks, and an analysis of limitations that constrain external validity: single LLM, synthetic/FRR‑based devices, emulator fidelity, and potential training‑data overlap. We conclude that, in the controlled emulation and task-generation regime studied, a verifier‑in‑the‑loop repair stage did not improve the verifier‑measured semantic correctness because the model and task generator produced verifier‑valid outputs at baseline; thus future work should focus on broader model families, vendor‑diverse device images, and adversarial or naturally noisy intent sets to reveal practical failure modes and the true marginal utility of verifier‑guided repair.

sections.introduction: Motivation and research question. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate operator intent into device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Prior surveys and benchmarks argue that the reliability of such agentic pipelines hinges on external validators, closed‑loop execution, and repair stages that catch and remove semantic errors before deployment [Brown et al.; OpsEval; NetConfArena]. However, the practical effect size of a verifier‑in‑the‑loop (generate–validate–repair) architecture on end‑to‑end semantic correctness in realistic multi‑device change tasks is not settled. We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to answer the research question: To what extent does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier (Batfish) reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device network configurations when tested in an emulation‑grounded closed loop?
sections.related_work: LLMs for NetOps have been surveyed and instantiated in intent‑translation and agentic remediation proposals; recent work emphasizes the necessity of tool‑assisted validation and closed‑loop evaluation (e.g., Batfish lessons [Brown et al.], OpsEval, NetConfArena). Research on verifier‑guided generation and verifier‑grounded repair has shown promise in domains where small syntactic fixes or verifier counterexamples can be used to drive corrections (e.g., verifier‑guided CTL/NuSMV workflows). Security reviews and benchmarks highlight execution realism and evaluation traceability as persistent gaps. Our study situates itself at the intersection of these threads by experimentally measuring the marginal effect of a bounded verifier‑guided repair loop under a preregistered paired design and emulation evaluation.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental design. We preregistered the study (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) and froze: the research question, primary confirmatory hypotheses, sampling plan (N=200 paired confirmatory intents stratified by topology cluster: 2‑device, 3–4 devices, 5–8 devices), inclusion/exclusion rules, timeouts, retry and missingness policies, and the exact primary analysis (paired McNemar test; bootstrap CI for absolute paired difference). The model used was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) with a single shared initial generation per intent and up to one verifier‑guided repair iteration under the guarded condition. The execution adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The pipeline components and constraints (public FRRouting/VyOS images for emulation, Batfish as the verifier, deterministic task generator for intent→reference mappings) were fixed before execution. We recorded all raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, deterministic contamination checks (exact SHA‑256 matches and n‑gram overlap flags), and artifact hashes; the preregistration manifest and execution manifest are archived.
sections.results: Execution summary and confirmatory outcome. The run completed as planned (execution manifest: 200 paired confirmatory intents, 400 completed episodes — baseline + guarded, zero failed episodes). Per the deterministic validator and the preregistered scoring rule (verifier pass = no Batfish violations and emulator‑observed reachability/policy satisfaction), both baseline and guarded conditions produced 200/200 verifier‑pass outcomes. The paired contingency table was n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; the estimated absolute paired success‑rate difference (guarded minus baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the absolute difference = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). Secondary planned estimands (iterations‑to‑pass statistics, syntactic‑executable differences) were vacuous because no repairs were applied: the baseline candidate was already verifier‑passing in each confirmatory case. Exploratory questions intended to study topology dependence and root causes were constrained by this ceiling effect; exploratory reserve intents remain archived for future adversarial or multi‑model follow‑ups.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The preregistered confirmatory result is a null effect: the verifier‑guided repair stage did not change verifier‑measured correctness because the single‑pass LLM outputs already satisfied the formal verifier and emulator tests in our controlled environment and task generation regime. This outcome has two valid interpretations that are not mutually exclusive: (1) under the chosen synthetic task generator, device images (FRR/VyOS), and with gpt‑5‑mini, the posed multi‑device intents were within the model's reliable generation capability as exercised here; (2) the evaluation regime (task difficulty distribution, emulator fidelity, device model set) may have been insufficiently challenging to expose typical operational failure modes where verifier‑guided repair would add value. Operational implication: verifier‑in‑the‑loop pipelines remain essential engineering practice because our results do not generalize beyond the constrained experimental scope; they do not imply that verification is unnecessary in production. Evidence provenance and reproducibility. We archive raw responses, validator traces, model‑call manifests, and the preregistration hash (preregistration_sha256=163150627c4bd8d1e2520caeaa8ac0f4e0aa78876c16c3246e91596c632e49ec).
sections.conclusion: We carried out a preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment assessing the marginal benefit of a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop repair stage for NL→config translation in an emulation setting. Under the exact controlled conditions studied (gpt‑5‑mini, FRR/VyOS emulation, deterministic synthetic intent generator), baseline single‑pass outputs already passed a formal verifier (Batfish) for all confirmatory tasks; consequently the guarded pipeline showed no improvement on the preregistered primary metric. This null result highlights the methodological lesson that task selection, device diversity, model heterogeneity, and adversarial or naturally noisy intents are crucial to meaningfully evaluate verifier‑guided repair. Future work should broaden model and device diversity, incorporate vendor‑specific images and real operator‑authored intents, and include adversarial intent perturbations and human‑operator approval workflows to reveal practical failure modes and quantify the operational value of verifier‑guided repair loops.

limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or vendors.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images). Real vendor quirks may expose additional failure modes.
Synthetic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture the full ambiguity, diversity, or adversarial distribution of real operator intents or legacy runbooks.

Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies or timing/race conditions of production devices; correctness under emulation may not imply production safety.
Ceiling effect in confirmatory cohort: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the verifier for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inferences.

Contamination risk: deterministic exact‑hash checks were applied and no exact matches were found in confirmatory N, but undetected paraphrase overlap between task generator outputs and LLM training data could remain.
Security and adversary scenarios: the study did not evaluate prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, or adversarial telemetry perturbations; such threat models remain an open concern.
